title: Stream client abstractions, event transformers, and fine-grained retry surface for Python SDK
creator: Claire Morrison
description:
Goal: provide a concise, composable streaming client abstraction for Python that exposes an event-transform pipeline and a configurable, per-event retry surface. This ticket defines API shapes, backpressure-friendly iterator semantics, and example patterns for downstream apps to transform streaming chat events into higher-level messages while controlling retries at the event level (delta, retry whole request, or skip).

Background: customers building conversational UIs need simple patterns to: (1) incrementally render choice and content tokens, (2) attach metadata (source/trace) to events, and (3) recover gracefully from transient transport or protocol errors without losing partial user-visible state. Existing SDK experiments provide low-level event feeds or raw SSE wrappers; we want a developer-facing pipeline with transformers, light checkpoint hooks, and an explicit retry API that does not force full request restarts by default.

Non-goals: this ticket does not implement persistence-backed checkpoints, nor complex server-side resume protocols. It also does not change the wire protocol between service and SDK.
acceptance_criteria: New StreamClient type available in python SDK (async-first) that yields typed Event objects
EventTransform API that can map/augment/filter events and can be composed via + or pipeline() helper
RetrySurface with granular policies: per-event (e.g., token-append retry), per-stream fallback (restart), and a 'resume-if-compatible' fast-path
Backpressure-friendly iterator: consumer controls read window and can request 'n' events or use time-based draining
Example notebook and two small samples in examples/ showing: (a) streaming UI rendering using transforms, (b) replay-and-correct flow after transient error
Unit tests covering transformers, retry decisions, and a simulated transport interruption scenario
implementation_notes:
API sketch (async):

from redwood import StreamClient, Event, EventTransform, RetryPolicy

async with StreamClient(model='rw-text-1') as client:
    async for evt in client.stream_chat(request, transforms=[add_trace, html_escape]):
        if evt.type == 'delta':
            render_incremental(evt.text)
        elif evt.type == 'choice':
            show_choice_button(evt.choice_id)

Key pieces:
- StreamClient.stream_chat(..., transforms=[...], retry_policy=RetryPolicy(...)) returns an async iterator of Event objects.
- EventTransform: callable(Event) -> Optional[Event]. Returning None drops the event. Transforms run in order and must be sync/async aware.
- RetryPolicy: object describing per-event decisions: retry_token_append, retry_entire_stream, skip_event. Policy is consulted when a transport or parse error occurs.

Performance considerations:
- Transform pipeline runs on consumer thread to avoid blocking runtime internals. Keep transforms cheap; expose a transform_executor hook to offload heavy work to threadpool.
- Minimal allocations for Event wrapper; underlying payload stays bytes until first read.

Telemetry hooks:
- emit stream.start/stream.error/stream.resume events with reason tags and traces (link to console traces).
Proposed module layout: redwood/stream/client.py, redwood/stream/transforms.py, redwood/stream/retries.py, examples/streaming_transformer_demo.py
Backward compatibility: existing low-level 'raw_stream' entrypoint kept; StreamClient is additive and should be recommended for new users
risks: Complexity of transform API could encourage heavy CPU work on event path and degrade latency
Ambiguous retry semantics might lead applications to inadvertently duplicate user-visible tokens if they reapply transforms on replay
Edge cases around partial JSON events (structured output) when a transform mutates the payload; need canonicalization guidelines
testing_plan: Unit: simulate transport layer that emits an interruption at N tokens; verify RetryPolicy choices are honored and transformed output is idempotent when required
Integration: run example app against staging with small models and inject network flaps to validate resume vs restart behaviors
Load: smoke benchmark to ensure transform pipeline adds <5% CPU and <1ms median per-event overhead for no-op transforms
Fuzz: random sequence of event types to validate event filter and drop behaviors
